abstract: The evolution of human skeletal morphology involved modifications to conserved developmental programs, but the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomic atlases of developing human, macaque and mouse limbs with comparative chromatin interaction maps of chondrocytes. We identify human-biased transcriptional programs within conserved osteochondral lineages and link divergent chromatin interactions to human-specific sequence changes. These analyses identify zooHAR.30, a human accelerated region that contacts the promoter of FOXC1, a key regulator of skeletal development. Human-specific substitutions within zooHAR.30 alter transcription factor binding, and the human sequence exhibits enhanced regulatory activity in chondrocytes and more spatially restricted activity in the developing limb, predominantly in the zeugopod, compared with the chimpanzee ortholog. Replacing the endogenous human sequence with its chimpanzee ortholog reduces FOXC1 and GMDS expression, impairs cell proliferation and osteochondral differentiation, and alters FOXC1 occupancy across skeletal regulatory elements, including a GDF5 enhancer implicated in knee morphology and osteoarthritis. Our findings reveal how evolutionary changes in a single enhancer can propagate through a conserved developmental regulatory network, providing a mechanistic link between human-specific sequence divergence and the evolution of skeletal developmental programs.
